extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy (Plato/Republic) and those studying ethical/political argumentation
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and examination of competing definitions of justice as presented in a Socratic dialogue (Plato's Republic). The passage develops standards for forming and testing definitions, uses analogies to arts, and assesses moral and political claims by logical and consequence-based tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and accuracy in definition
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I must have clearness and accuracy.’ (Thrasymachus demands ‘clearness and accuracy’ in any definition.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions must be stated in precise senses; avoid vague or colloquial usages. Socrates presses for precise meanings and shows how imprecision (e.g., forbidding certain obvious answers) blocks genuine understanding. In practice, require that key terms be unambiguous before proceeding with argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must withstand counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed definition ‘to speak the truth and to pay your debts’ is shown to fail by counterexample (returning deposited arms to a friend who is not in his right mind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test any candidate definition with hypothetical or extreme cases to reveal exceptions. If a definition yields an absurd or unacceptable conclusion in a plausible case, it must be revised or rejected. Thought experiments and concrete scenarios are appropriate tools for this testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate justice with doing good to friends and harm to enemies without qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Polemarchus/Simonides: ‘justice is the giving to each man what is proper to him’ or ‘doing good to friends and harm to enemies.’ Socrates and others show problems with this when ‘friends’/‘enemies’ are only seeming, and when injury makes people worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether ‘friend’ and ‘enemy’ refer to apparent or actual moral character. Evaluate whether a proposed moral rule (do good to friends/harm enemies) conflicts with broader moral principles (e.g., harming makes people worse) and whether it yields contradictions when applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts/rulership aim at the good of their subjects, not the ruler’s private interest
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘No science or art considers or enjoins the interest of the stronger or superior, but only the interest of the subject and weaker’ — medicine cares for the body, horsemanship for the horse, pilot for sailors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining the purpose or ethics of a craft, office, or institution, identify the proper subject-matter and treat the art as oriented toward that subject’s good. Use examples (medicine, navigation, horsemanship) to check that purported aims align with the true function of the art/office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equivocation and inconsistent use of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates points out Thrasymachus’s inconsistent use of the word ‘interest’ (forbidding it then using it) and the shifting sense of ‘ruler’/‘stronger.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep term meanings stable throughout an argument. Watch for covert shifts in sense (e.g., popular vs. strict senses of a role) that permit fallacious moves. Demand that interlocutors define important words and stick to those definitions unless they explicitly revise them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish strict (function-based) from popular senses of roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion distinguishes a true ruler/pilot/physician ‘in the strict sense’ (whose function is to benefit the subject) from mere appearances or title-holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about offices, skills, or virtues, specify whether you mean the ideal/expert (strict) or the ordinary/popular sense. Many paradoxes dissolve when roles are treated in their functional, not merely nominal, senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogies to arts to clarify ethical/political concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates draws analogies to medicine, cookery, shoemaking, husbandry, pilots, and horsemen to probe what ‘due’ or ‘proper’ means and to test the idea of justice as a technical art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies can illuminate the proper object and function of a concept (e.g., justice as an art). Ensure the analogy maps relevant structural features and be explicit about where the analogy stops working. Use multiple analogies to triangulate a concept’s function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess moral claims by their consequences for virtue and human flourishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that injuring a person makes them worse in their proper virtues (e.g., a horse injured is worse as a horse); since justice is a human virtue, justice cannot consist in harming others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral definitions by whether they promote or degrade the virtues proper to human nature. If a conception of justice entails making people morally worse, that is a strong reason to reject it. Consider normative consequences (character formation, civic health) as part of the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive positive accounts, not only refutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrasymachus criticises merely asking questions and refuting others: one should answer and give one’s own account rather than only knocking down opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In philosophical and creative argumentation, pair critique with constructive proposals. After exposing flaws in a definition, supply an alternative that addresses the identified problems. This is a standard of dialectical rigor in the dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test political/moral definitions against variability of institutions and ruler fallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrasymachus’s claim that ‘justice is the interest of the stronger’ is tested by noting governments differ and rulers may err when making laws; thus justice cannot simply be obedience to rulers’ commands without qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining justice or social norms, account for differences in political forms and the possibility of mistaken legislation or corrupt rulers. A robust definition should not collapse into mere conformity with whoever holds power; include criteria that survive institutional variability.
